title: DFS & BFS
description: Problems solvable using both Depth-First Search and Breadth-First Search traversals on graphs.
identify: The problem involves traversing or exploring a grid/graph.
The problem asks to find connected regions, count components, or fill areas.
explanation: DFS explores as deep as possible before backtracking, while BFS explores neighbors level by level. Both can solve traversal problems, but DFS is simpler to implement recursively and BFS naturally finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

title: Cycles
description: Detecting cycles in undirected and directed graphs using DFS/BFS techniques.
identify: The problem asks if a cycle exists in a graph.
The problem involves checking bipartiteness or detecting back edges.
explanation: In undirected graphs, a cycle is detected when we visit a node that's already visited and is NOT the parent. In directed graphs, we use DFS with a recursion stack — a back edge to a node in the current stack indicates a cycle.

title: BFS
description: Multi-source BFS and shortest path problems in unweighted graphs and grids.
identify: The problem involves finding the shortest distance in an unweighted graph or grid.
The problem involves spreading or propagation from multiple sources simultaneously.
explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level, making it ideal for finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Multi-source BFS starts from all sources simultaneously, processing them in waves.

title: BFS Hard
description: Advanced BFS problems involving word transformations and complex state spaces.
identify: The problem involves transforming one state to another with minimum steps.
Each transformation changes a small part of the current state.
explanation: These problems model each state as a node in an implicit graph. BFS finds the shortest transformation sequence since each transformation is one edge.

title: Topological Sort
description: Ordering vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that every edge u→v has u before v.
identify: The problem involves ordering tasks with dependencies.
The problem is on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
explanation: Topological Sort can be done via DFS (using a stack to store nodes after all descendants are processed) or BFS (Kahn's Algorithm using indegree). It only works on DAGs.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
description: Finding shortest paths in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights.
identify: The problem asks for shortest path in a weighted graph.
All edge weights are non-negative.
explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm is a greedy algorithm that finds shortest paths from a source to all vertices. It uses a min-heap to always process the closest unvisited vertex first. It does NOT work with negative edge weights.

title: Bellman-Ford & Floyd-Warshall
description: Shortest path algorithms handling negative edge weights, negative cycle detection, and all-pairs shortest paths.
identify: The graph contains negative weights or requires negative cycle detection (Bellman-Ford).
The problem requires finding shortest distances between all pairs of vertices or threshold reachability across all nodes (Floyd-Warshall).
appearsIn: Negative cycle detection in financial networks
explanation: Bellman-Ford works on directed graphs with negative weights and detects negative cycles by relaxing all edges V-1 times. Floyd-Warshall is a dynamic programming algorithm computing all-pairs shortest paths by evaluating paths via every intermediate vertex k in O(V^3) time.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
description: Finding a tree that connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight.
identify: The problem asks to connect all nodes with minimum cost.
The problem involves selecting edges to form a spanning tree.
explanation: An MST connects all vertices in a weighted undirected graph with the minimum possible total edge weight. Prim's algorithm grows the tree greedily from a source, while Kruskal's sorts edges and adds them if they don't form a cycle (using Union-Find).

title: Disjoint Set (Union-Find)
description: A data structure to efficiently track connected components and merge sets.
identify: The problem involves dynamic connectivity queries.
The problem asks to merge groups or check if two elements belong to the same set.
explanation: Disjoint Set Union (DSU) supports two operations: Find (which component does an element belong to?) and Union (merge two components). With path compression and union by rank, both operations run in nearly O(1) amortized time.

title: Advanced Graph Algorithms
description: Critical graph decomposition algorithms including Tarjan's bridge and articulation point algorithms, and Kosaraju's algorithm for strongly connected components.
identify: The problem asks for critical edges or vertices whose removal disconnects the graph.
The problem asks to decompose a directed graph into components where every vertex can reach every other vertex.
explanation: Tarjan's algorithm uses DFS discovery times (tin) and lowest reachable times (low) to detect bridges (low[v] > tin[u]) and articulation points (low[v] >= tin[u]). Kosaraju's algorithm finds SCCs in directed graphs using a 2-pass DFS: first ordering by finishing times, then reversing edges and traversing components.
